Cyclists at risk

By: Laura Byrne | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A high-profile attack on a cyclist has raised public awareness of increasing violent crime

Unique Selling Point:
The latest and one of the most violent attacks on a cyclist took place in the Cradle of Humankind last Saturday. An unidentified cyclist (Jim) was shot twice by men who then drove away with his bicycle. In an act of heroism that has captured the imagination of the country, passerby Jon Jon Pietersen stopped to help and with nothing more than a single glove, a towel and some tape, stopped the bleeding long enough for Jim to be airlifted to hospital. Pietersen's heroism might restore faith in humanity - but the dark truth is that cyclists are increasingly at risk on our roads and off them. And it seems police and society alike are powerless to stop the escalating violence.

Summary:
Bike jacking and bike theft have become quite commonplace as more and more South Africans take part in this expensive and increasingly popular sport, and criminals realise the potential for a quick buck. Many speculate that the thieves are organised by syndicates selling bikes outside the country. With little real data on the size of the problem, cyclists rely on social media to find stolen bikes and raise community awareness about their vulnerability. Forums are littered with reports of stolen bicycles and awareness campaigns seek to educate both cyclists and motorists. But on a regular basis the stakes are raised by stories of escalating violence.

In the latest such story, which has made news headlines, 'Jim' was accosted while riding alone in the Cradle on Saturday morning (11 August) and shot twice by men who then took his bike and shoes and escaped in a bakkie. Mere minutes later, hobbyist hiker Jon Jon Pietersen and his friend came across Jim lying on the side of the road. Pietersen had been out scouting for new locations for his hiking club, and they had decided to drive past the spot to see the white tiger kept at the Rhino and Lion park. It was pure chance that Jon Jon heard Jim's call for help. They immediately stopped and with the help of a second motorist, Jon Jon tried to stop Jim's bleeding using a single surgical glove, a towel and some tape. Miraculously, he managed to keep Jim alive until the ambulance arrived 20 minutes later. Jim is now recovering at home.

Further information:
As cycling increases in popularity, cyclists become more and more vulnerable to hit and run incidents, burglary and increasingly violent crime. Mountain bikers are accosted on the trail and pushed off their bikes. Road cyclists are stopped by men in cars - in one incident, a group of 10 people were stopped in the Western Cape.Even safety in numbers has become a myth. Groups like the Pedal Power Association try to raise awareness and advise members on riding safely, but they are powerless to do much. An expensive bike can cost upwards of R100 000 - far outside the budget of an Alex commuter - so where are the bikes going? Some speculate there are syndicate selling them in China or Mozambique. Others suggest they are being stripped for parts and sold to unsuspecting buyers on Bike Hub and Gumtree. With no licence plates or VIN numbers, they are almost impossible to track, and tracking devices are heavy and cumbersome. And with so many crimes on their books, the police are not always willing to put in the manpower to help.

Jim is not willing to speak to us but his daughter Raquel is.

Jon Jon will speak to us about his experience saving Jim's life. He will meet us in the Cradle to show us the spot. We will also do a reenactment.

We are not able to speak to the Netcare 911 paramedic who was on the scene, as Jim refused permission.

The PPA will give their perspective on the growing problem and what is being done to address it. Cycling South Africa will also speak.

Press Release:


Cyclists at Risk
Could your expensive, state-of-the-art bicycle cost you your life? Recently a leisurely cycle turned into a near death experience for one Johannesburg cyclist, after he was shot and left on the side of the road. But the quick actions of a good Samaritan helped save his life. Exposed and vulnerable, a growing number of cyclists have fallen victim to these violent attacks and the theft of their bicycles.
Producer: Laura Byrne
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


VO1: Last weekend, a vicious attack left a Joburg cyclist in hospital with two gunshot wounds. The story hit national headlines.
UPSOUND Raquel McPhee: I was at my mom’s house. And my brother’s phone rang and he answered the phone and it was my dad saying boy I’ve just been shot. I’m in hospital.
LINK: An ordinary Saturday morning. A peaceful scene in the Cradle of Humankind just outside Joburg. Jim was just one of the hundreds of cyclists who flock here weekly – little did he know that this Saturday would almost end with his death.
VO2: Jim was still too traumatised to speak to us this week – but we met his daughter Raquel at work to hear the story.
UPSOUND: Raquel McPhee: He was out on his bike every day, cycling the same route every day because he is an avid triathlete.
VO3: Jim was riding alone on Kromdraai Road, his first time back on the bike after an injury.
UPSOUND: Raquel McPhee: A vehicle got too close and pushed him off the road.
VO4: As Jim tried to regain his balance, three men approached.
UPSOUND: Raquel McPhee: They pulled his bicycle away from him. He then fought back. And it was then that he was shot the first time in the leg.
VO5: The men shot Jim a second time through the torso, stole his helmet, shoes and watch and left him to die.
UPSOUND: Raquel McPhee: After that, a car came past and that was the guy that saved his life.
VO6: The Good Samaritan was Jon Jon Pietersen.
UPSOUND Jon Jon Pietersen: I was driving around with my friend. We were looking for hiking spots. I heard a guy shout help me. I’m not going to lie to you, the first thing I did was think, wow, this is a trap. I then looked and I saw the blood coming out the back of his leg. The first thing that kicked in is I need to stop the bleeding, I need to apply some pressure. I didn’t have any gloves so I put my foot on the wound.
VO7: And so began a surreal struggle to save Jim’s life using nothing more than a broken pair of surgical gloves, a towel, tape and some gauze.
UPSOUND: Jon-Jon Pietersen: There’s no first aid kit. You don’t know who’s in the bushes around you. While it was happening it felt like two hours. When people say time slowed down, it really slowed down. I now know it was 20 minutes.
VO8: With the help of passers-by, Jon-Jon stopped the bleeding long enough for Jim to be airlifted to hospital.
UPSOUND: Raquel McPhee: I just can’t express how thankful we are. That I can go home to a dad. That my son can have his grandfather.
UPSOUND: Jon-Jon Pietersen: He was very grateful. It kind of hit me hard. And he said I want to say thank you that I can hold my son again.
VO9: Jim was discharged from hospital on Tuesday and is recovering at home. But the cycling community is still reeling from the brutality of the latest in a string of attacks.
VOX POP 1: It spoils the fun that we have because you end up anxious about what’s going to happen.
VOX POP 2: Recently we’ve been hearing a lot of stories. It’s not safe anymore.
VOX POP 4: I would be lying to say it doesn’t concern me.
LINK: In the past decade, the popularity of cycling in SA has exploded. Every week, thousands of devotees don their lycra and helmets and take to the great outdoors. It’s sociable, it’s healthy – but increasingly cyclists are facing the most ubiquitous of South African woes: violent crime.
UPSOUND: Rolf Weber: It was a regular Saturday, friend and I went for a ride.
VO10: Rolf Weber was attacked at Riversands, a popular area for mountain bikers north of Johannesburg.
UPSOUND: Rolf Weber: The one guy had a gun. There was a guy in front of me and another one with a steel pipe and he started smashing me on the head.
UPSOUND: Jon Heeger: The bike jacker and I just happened to be on the same path moving in different directions at the same time. He had the gun, I had the bike.
VO11: Jon Heeger has been bike jacked twice at gunpoint, within metres of his home in Midrand.
UPSOUND: Jon Heeger: The second occasion there were two of them and I think it was a carefully planned ambush.
VO12: Phillip Ralehlaka was held up at gunpoint one evening riding alone in Centurion.
UPSOUND: Philip Ralehlaka: It’s like you‘re going into the jungle. You need to carry a firearm when you’re going cycling now. You need to carry something, some sort of a weapon to arm yourself. And what kind of sport will that be?
VO13: The police count bike jacking as part of community related crime, which includes everything from house breaking to murder.
LINK: No one has real statistics. But popular opinion is that these attacks are growing in number and violence.
VO14: Riding in isolated areas, on bikes ranging from tens to hundreds of thousands in value, cyclists are attractive targets. This week we were inundated with stories from the community – many of whom now carry weapons to protect themselves. In some cases, attacks have even resulted in death.
VOX POP 5: These days I cycle with a Taser in my pocket. On our Wednesday group if there’s not more than 4 or 5 of us they cancel the ride.
UPSOUND: Robert Vogel: We all say ride in a group if possible. But we’ve seen groups have been attacked, so we can’t even say you’re safe in a group any more.
VO15: Robert Vogel is CEO of the non-profit Pedal Power Association.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What is law enforcement’s attitude to these attacks?
Robert Vogel: I think they don’t take it seriously enough. We’ve got to try and keep the pressure on the authorities to follow through with these cases so we can get one all the way through, with an outcome, with a conviction.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: And have the police given you any feedback?
Jon Heeger: No. what chance have they got? There was no evidence.
VO16: Police told us there is no indication of a growing trend in bike jacking, and that attacks are merely opportunistic. They say aggravated robbery is always treated as a priority crime.
UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: I’m going to say that these attacks on cyclists are just an example of the South African general crime problem.
VO17: Steve Saunders spoke to us on behalf of Cycling South Africa.
UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: Whether the person is riding a R200 bicycle or a R200 000 bicycle is irrelevant if it got stolen from them.
LINK: Where are these bicycles going? Theories range from second hand sales online to international criminal syndicates. The truth is, no one knows – but bikes are in plentiful supply and for the thieves, the risks are almost non-existent.
UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: If cycling is not safe, our organised activities and the sport in general are under threat.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: You say that he loves cycling. Do you think he would ever cycle again after this?
Raquel McPhee: In his words now, no. He will not get back onto a bicycle.
UPSOUND: Rolf Weber: I have a son who’s two weeks old. When I go riding in the morning now, it’s in the back of my mind, I have a family I need to make sure I come home to.
VO18: It’s not only violent crime that makes many think twice about getting on a bike. Hostility from drivers also jeopardises cycling as a viable alternative to motorised transport.
UPSOUND: Robert Vogel: It alleviates congestion. It’s great for the environment. Great for your personal health. It gets you around a lot quicker in urban centres than a car does these days. But we need that environment that encourages the uptake of cycling.
VO19: So what is the solution?
UPSOUND: Robert Vogel: We’re all on that road together. Cyclists are allowed to use the roads. They’re a legal road user. I think what we all need to do is just respect each other’s humanity.
VO20: The Cradle community is implementing visible security and emergency response teams. For the cyclists it’s a toss-up between staying safe and doing what they love.
UPSOUND: Phillip Ralehlaka: It has changed how I view cycling now. I’m no longer going to cycle by myself when it’s dark.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Are you still riding?
Rolf Weber: Yep, still out there, still riding.
Claire Mawisa: Why?
Rolf Weber: It’s my hobby. It’s my passion, it’s my little bit of freedom.
VOX POP 3: I keep myself fit. With the age that I’m at as well you need something as well to stay young.
UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: I think the worst thing we can do is to retract from the environment. I think the best thing we can do is get involved in that environment.
VOX POP 4: It’s something I love, something that I enjoy doing. I’m going to carry on doing it, but just try and look out for all the hazards around and try to be as safe as I could possibly be.

10 SECOND PROMO
This week a vicious robbery left a Joburg cyclist in hospital with two gunshot wounds. Are violent attacks on cyclists a growing trend?

15 SECOND PROMO
VOX POP 2: Recently we’ve been hearing a lot of stories. It’s not safe anymore.
VO: A cyclist was viciously robbed and shot in the Cradle of Humankind this week. Is this attack part of a growing trend?
UPSOUND: VOX POP 1: You end up anxious about what’s going to happen.

15 SECOND PROMO
UPSOUND Raquel McPhee: [21:00] I just can’t express how thankful we are.
VO: A cyclist’s life was dramatically saved this week after he was shot in the Cradle of Humankind. The community says violent crime is on the increase.
UPSOUND: VOX POP 5: These days I cycle with a Taser in my pocket.

30 SECOND PROMO
LINK: In the past decade, the popularity of cycling in SA has exploded. Every weekend, thousands of devotees don their lycra and helmets and take to the great outdoors.
VOX POP 4: It’s something I love, something that I enjoy doing.
VO: But this week a vicious robbery in the Cradle of Humankind drew national attention to cyclists’ vulnerability to violent crime.
UPSOUND Raquel McPhee: My brother’s phone rang. And he answered the phone and it was my dad saying boy I’ve just been shot. I’m in hospital.

LINK: In the past decade, the popularity of cycling in SA has exploded. Every week, thousands of devotees don their lycra and helmets and take to the great outdoors. It’s sociable, it’s healthy – but increasingly cyclists are facing the most ubiquitous of South African woes: violent crime. UPSOUND: Rolf Weber: It was a regular Saturday, friend and I went for a ride. VO10: Rolf Weber was attacked at Riversands, a popular area for mountain bikers north of Johannesburg. UPSOUND: Rolf Weber: The one guy had a gun. There was a guy in front of me and another one with a steel pipe and he started smashing me on the head. UPSOUND: Jon Heeger: The bike jacker and I just happened to be on the same path moving in different directions at the same time. He had the gun, I had the bike. VO11: Jon Heeger has been bike jacked twice at gunpoint, within metres of his home in Midrand. UPSOUND: Jon Heeger: The second occasion there were two of them and I think it was a carefully planned ambush. VO12: Phillip Ralehlaka was held up at gunpoint one evening riding alone in Centurion. UPSOUND: Philip Ralehlaka: It’s like you‘re going into the jungle. You need to carry a firearm when you’re going cycling now. You need to carry something, some sort of a weapon to arm yourself. And what kind of sport will that be? VO13: The police count bike jacking as part of community related crime, which includes everything from house breaking to murder. LINK: No one has real statistics. But popular opinion is that these attacks are growing in number and violence. VO14: Riding in isolated areas, on bikes ranging from tens to hundreds of thousands in value, cyclists are attractive targets. This week we were inundated with stories from the community – many of whom now carry weapons to protect themselves. In some cases, attacks have even resulted in death. VOX POP 5: These days I cycle with a Taser in my pocket. On our Wednesday group if there’s not more than 4 or 5 of us they cancel the ride. UPSOUND: Robert Vogel: We all say ride in a group if possible. But we’ve seen groups have been attacked, so we can’t even say you’re safe in a group any more. VO15: Robert Vogel is CEO of the non-profit Pedal Power Association. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What is law enforcement’s attitude to these attacks? Robert Vogel: I think they don’t take it seriously enough. We’ve got to try and keep the pressure on the authorities to follow through with these cases so we can get one all the way through, with an outcome, with a conviction. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: And have the police given you any feedback? Jon Heeger: No. what chance have they got? There was no evidence. VO16: Police told us there is no indication of a growing trend in bike jacking, and that attacks are merely opportunistic. They say aggravated robbery is always treated as a priority crime. UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: I’m going to say that these attacks on cyclists are just an example of the South African general crime problem. VO17: Steve Saunders spoke to us on behalf of Cycling South Africa. UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: Whether the person is riding a R200 bicycle or a R200 000 bicycle is irrelevant if it got stolen from them. LINK: Where are these bicycles going? Theories range from second hand sales online to international criminal syndicates. The truth is, no one knows – but bikes are in plentiful supply and for the thieves, the risks are almost non-existent. UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: If cycling is not safe, our organised activities and the sport in general are under threat. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: You say that he loves cycling. Do you think he would ever cycle again after this? Raquel McPhee: In his words now, no. He will not get back onto a bicycle. UPSOUND: Rolf Weber: I have a son who’s two weeks old. When I go riding in the morning now, it’s in the back of my mind, I have a family I need to make sure I come home to. VO18: It’s not only violent crime that makes many think twice about getting on a bike. Hostility from drivers also jeopardises cycling as a viable alternative to motorised transport. UPSOUND: Robert Vogel: It alleviates congestion. It’s great for the environment. Great for your personal health. It gets you around a lot quicker in urban centres than a car does these days. But we need that environment that encourages the uptake of cycling. VO19: So what is the solution? UPSOUND: Robert Vogel: We’re all on that road together. Cyclists are allowed to use the roads. They’re a legal road user. I think what we all need to do is just respect each other’s humanity. VO20: The Cradle community is implementing visible security and emergency response teams. It’s my passion, it’s my little bit of freedom. VOX POP 3: I keep myself fit. With the age that I’m at as well you need something as well to stay young. UPSOUND: Steve Saunders: I think the worst thing we can do is to retract from the environment. I think the best thing we can do is get involved in that environment. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A high-profile attack on a cyclist has raised public awareness of increasing violent crime
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The latest and one of the most violent attacks on a cyclist took place in the Cradle of Humankind last Saturday. An unidentified cyclist (Jim) was shot twice by men who then drove away with his bicycle. In an act of heroism that has captured the imagination of the country, passerby Jon Jon Pietersen stopped to help and with nothing more than a single glove, a towel and some tape, stopped the bleeding long enough for Jim to be airlifted to hospital. Pietersen's heroism might restore faith in humanity - but the dark truth is that cyclists are increasingly at risk on our roads and off them. And it seems police and society alike are powerless to stop the escalating violence.
metadata.Summary: Bike jacking and bike theft have become quite commonplace as more and more South Africans take part in this expensive and increasingly popular sport, and criminals realise the potential for a quick buck. Many speculate that the thieves are organised by syndicates selling bikes outside the country. With little real data on the size of the problem, cyclists rely on social media to find stolen bikes and raise community awareness about their vulnerability. Forums are littered with reports of stolen bicycles and awareness campaigns seek to educate both cyclists and motorists. But on a regular basis the stakes are raised by stories of escalating violence. In the latest such story, which has made news headlines, 'Jim' was accosted while riding alone in the Cradle on Saturday morning (11 August) and shot twice by men who then took his bike and shoes and escaped in a bakkie. Mere minutes later, hobbyist hiker Jon Jon Pietersen and his friend came across Jim lying on the side of the road. Pietersen had been out scouting for new locations for his hiking club, and they had decided to drive past the spot to see the white tiger kept at the Rhino and Lion park. It was pure chance that Jon Jon heard Jim's call for help. They immediately stopped and with the help of a second motorist, Jon Jon tried to stop Jim's bleeding using a single surgical glove, a towel and some tape. Miraculously, he managed to keep Jim alive until the ambulance arrived 20 minutes later. Jim is now recovering at home.
metadata.Further information: As cycling increases in popularity, cyclists become more and more vulnerable to hit and run incidents, burglary and increasingly violent crime. Mountain bikers are accosted on the trail and pushed off their bikes. Road cyclists are stopped by men in cars - in one incident, a group of 10 people were stopped in the Western Cape.Even safety in numbers has become a myth. Groups like the Pedal Power Association try to raise awareness and advise members on riding safely, but they are powerless to do much. An expensive bike can cost upwards of R100 000 - far outside the budget of an Alex commuter - so where are the bikes going? Some speculate there are syndicate selling them in China or Mozambique. Others suggest they are being stripped for parts and sold to unsuspecting buyers on Bike Hub and Gumtree. With no licence plates or VIN numbers, they are almost impossible to track, and tracking devices are heavy and cumbersome. And with so many crimes on their books, the police are not always willing to put in the manpower to help. Jim is not willing to speak to us but his daughter Raquel is. Jon Jon will speak to us about his experience saving Jim's life. He will meet us in the Cradle to show us the spot. We will also do a reenactment. We are not able to speak to the Netcare 911 paramedic who was on the scene, as Jim refused permission. The PPA will give their perspective on the growing problem and what is being done to address it. Cycling South Africa will also speak.
